analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans that cover mastectomies to also cover breast reconstruction surgery.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 19 Senate Democrats, was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required health plans and insurers that cover mastectomies to also cover reconstructive breast surgery, including surgery on the other breast for symmetry, external prostheses, and treatment of complications like lymphedema. It barred insurers from calling the surgery "cosmetic" to deny it, from offering women cash to give up the protection, and from penalizing doctors who provide the care. The requirements would have applied to employer plans, group insurance, and the individual insurance market.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who undergo mastectomies and their families. Instead of facing out-of-pocket bills for reconstruction — often tens of thousands of dollars — or going without, they would have had the surgery covered as a condition of the plan covering the mastectomy itself. Patients were also protected from being dropped, offered rebates to waive the coverage, or steered away from reconstruction by provider incentives. Doctors and hospitals performing reconstruction, and makers of breast prostheses, would have gained a larger pool of covered patients.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any group health plan or insurer that covers mastectomies to cover reconstruction of the diseased breast, surgery on the other breast to restore symmetry, prostheses, and mastectomy complications including lymphedema [S2][S3].

Prohibits insurers from denying the coverage as 'cosmetic' surgery, from dropping or refusing to enroll a woman to evade the requirement, and from offering women payments or rebates to accept less protection [S2][S3].

Protects doctors from reimbursement cuts or incentives designed to discourage them from providing the care, and applies the same rules to the individual insurance market, not just employer plans [S2][S3].
Caps cost-sharing for reconstruction at no more than what the plan charges for the mastectomy itself, and makes clear no woman can be forced to have the surgery [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor plans, through the added cost of covering reconstruction, prostheses, and complication care, which would be passed into premiums. The cost is limited: plans that do not cover mastectomies at all are exempt, and cost-sharing for reconstruction cannot exceed what the plan charges for mastectomy care [S3].

drawbacks.text: The mandate adds a required benefit to every plan that covers mastectomies, which would raise premiums — a real cost for small employers and people buying individual coverage, where the bill also applies the requirement [S3].

Critics of benefit mandates argue some women would prefer a cheaper plan without reconstruction coverage; the bill forecloses that choice by banning plans from offering rebates or payments to women who waive the protection [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and targeted at a frightening moment — a woman with breast cancer would no longer face a large bill, or a 'cosmetic surgery' denial, for reconstruction. The costs are real but modest and tightly scoped: only plans already covering mastectomies are affected, cost-sharing is capped at mastectomy parity, and insurers remain free to negotiate reimbursement rates with providers [S3]. On balance the design is fairly clean as mandates go, though it does raise premiums somewhat in the individual and small-group markets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never gave it a hearing or vote — it sat there until the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on April 17, 1997, joined by 18 Democratic cosponsors including Minority Leader Tom Daschle and Senators Mikulski, Boxer, and Murray [S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor action followed. The only recorded actions are introduction, introductory remarks, and the committee referral [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were better off because the bill died — they avoided the added cost of covering reconstruction, prostheses, and complication care for the remainder of the Congress, while women facing mastectomies got no federal guarantee from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers avoiding coverage costs

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and no recorded vote ever showed where the chambers stood.

industries.note: Any plan or policy covering mastectomies would have had to add reconstruction, symmetry surgery, prostheses, and complication care, with cost-sharing capped at mastectomy parity, and could not offer women rebates to waive the benefit. Insurers avoided this added cost when the bill died.
The bill amended ERISA to bind employer-sponsored plans directly, so employers would have borne higher benefits costs. No requirement applied to plans that do not cover mastectomies at all.
Reconstruction would have become a covered benefit rather than an out-of-pocket expense, expanding the pool of insured patients; the bill preserved insurers' freedom to negotiate reimbursement rates.
External prostheses would have been a required covered benefit for plans covering mastectomies, at cost-sharing no greater than for mastectomy care.
